tasks.title: Rolling the Dice
tasks.context: 5 fair six-sided dice are rolled at once, and the 5 results are recorded in order (each die is distinguishable).
statements: The total number of possible outcomes is 7,776.
The probability that all five dice show different numbers is greater than 20%.
The probability that at least two dice show the same number is less than 80%.
The probability that all five dice show different numbers equals exactly 1/6.
If only 3 dice were rolled instead of 5, the probability of all different values would be lower than with 5 dice.
tactical_explanations:
Statement A — True

Each of the 5 dice has 6 possible outcomes, independently, giving 6⁵ = 7,776 total outcomes.

$$
Total outcomes = 6⁵
$$

Takeaway: Each of the 5 dice has 6 possible outcomes, independently, giving 6⁵ = 7,776 total outcomes.

Statement B — False

P(all different) = 5/54 ≈ 9.26%, which is not greater than 20% — it is well below it.

$$
P(all different) = 6·5·4·3·2 / 6⁵
$$

Close call: P(all different) = 5/54 ≈ 9.26%, which is not greater than 20% — it is well below it.

Takeaway: P(all different) = 5/54 ≈ 9.26%, which is not greater than 20% — it is well below it.

Statement C — False

P(at least two the same) = 1 − 5/54 ≈ 90.74%, which is not less than 80% — it is considerably higher, since having any
repeat among 5 dice sharing only 6 faces is quite common (this is the same logic behind the birthday paradox).

$$
P(at least two same) = 1 − P(all different)
$$

Takeaway: P(at least two the same) = 1 − 5/54 ≈ 90.74%, which is not less than 80% — it is considerably higher, since having any
repeat among 5 dice sharing only 6 faces is quite common (this is the same logic behind the birthday paradox).

Statement D — False

P(all different) = 5/54 ≈ 0.0926, while 1/6 ≈ 0.1667.
These are not equal — a common error is to assume each die
independently has a 1/6 chance of "being different," but the constraint compounds across all 5 dice.

$$
Compare 5/54 to 1/6
$$

Takeaway: These are not equal — a common error is to assume each die
independently has a 1/6 chance of "being different," but the constraint compounds across all 5 dice.

With only 3 dice, P(all different) = 6·5·4/6³ = 120/216 ≈ 55.56%, which is much higher than the 9.26% found with 5 dice — not lower.
Fewer dice means less opportunity for a repeat, so the probability of all-different values goes up, not down,
when the number of dice decreases.

$$
Compare P(all different, 3 dice) ≈ 55.56% to P(all different, 5 dice) ≈ 9.26%
$$

Takeaway: Fewer dice means less opportunity for a repeat, so the probability of all-different values goes up, not down,
when the number of dice decreases.

tasks.title: Find the Missing Value
tasks.context: In a group of n people, every pair of people shakes hands exactly once. The total number of handshakes is 45.
statements: The unknown value n equals 10.
If the group had 12 people instead, the total number of handshakes would be 66.
The number of ways to choose a committee of 3 people from the n people is 120.
The number of ways to arrange all n people in a single row (n!) is greater than 1,000,000.
If the total number of handshakes had been 55 instead of 45, n would equal 11.
tactical_explanations:
Statement A — True

Solving Cn2 = 45 gives n(n−1) = 90, and n = 10 satisfies this (10·9 = 90), as found in Step 1.

$$
Solve \binom{n}{2} = 45 for n
$$

Takeaway: Solving Cn2 = 45 gives n(n−1) = 90, and n = 10 satisfies this (10·9 = 90), as found in Step 1.

Statement B — True

C122 = 12·11/2 = 66, confirming the statement.

$$
\binom{12}{2} = 12·11/2 = 66
$$

Takeaway: C122 = 12·11/2 = 66, confirming the statement.

Statement C — True

With n = 10, C103 = 10!/(3!·7!) = 120, confirming the statement.

$$
\binom{10}{3} = 10·9·8/3! = 120
$$

Takeaway: With n = 10, C103 = 10!/(3!·7!) = 120, confirming the statement.

Statement D — True

10! = 3,628,800, which is indeed greater than 1,000,000.

$$
10! = 3,628,800
$$

Takeaway: 10! = 3,628,800, which is indeed greater than 1,000,000.

Statement E — True

Solving Cn2 = 55 gives n(n−1) = 110, and n = 11 satisfies this (11·10 = 110), confirming the statement.

Tip: Two traps repeat across this set: (1) a ratio landing exactly on a round number (5, 6, 8, or 10) does not make a
"more than" or "less than" statement about that number true — check the direction carefully (Questions 2, 3).
(2)
Reducing the number of trials in a "no-repeats" probability (fewer dice, fewer cards, fewer people) always makes "all
different / no match" more likely, not less — repeats become harder to force with fewer draws (Question 5).

tasks.title: Chevalier de Méré's Dice Problem

The probability of rolling at least one double-six in 24 rolls of a pair of dice is greater than the probability of rolling at least one 6 in 4 rolls of a single die.

P(at least one 6 in 4 rolls) ≈ 51.77%, which is greater than 50% — this is the historical result that made betting on this
outcome profitable in the long run.

$$
P(at least one 6) = 1 − (5/6)⁴ ≈ 0.5177
$$

Takeaway: P(at least one 6 in 4 rolls) ≈ 51.77%, which is greater than 50% — this is the historical result that made betting on this
outcome profitable in the long run.

Statement B — True

This is exactly the complement-rule formula applied to 4 independent rolls, each with a 5/6 chance of avoiding a 6.

$$
P(at least one 6 in 4 rolls) = 1 − (5/6)⁴
$$

Takeaway: This is exactly the complement-rule formula applied to 4 independent rolls, each with a 5/6 chance of avoiding a 6.

Statement C — False

P(no 6 at all) = (5/6)⁴ ≈ 48.23%, which is not less than 45% — it is higher.

$$
P(no 6 in 4 rolls) = (5/6)⁴
$$

Takeaway: P(no 6 at all) = (5/6)⁴ ≈ 48.23%, which is not less than 45% — it is higher.

$$
